segments.title: The Squeal Heard 'Round Thanksgiving: Tom Brady Loses It in the Booth
segments.why_trending: Tom Brady let out a high-pitched, drawn-out squeal on the Fox broadcast as Jake Elliott's 59-yard field goal with 2 seconds left finished off the Eagles' 39-38 comeback win over the Cowboys. The Boston Globe said the clip had more than six million views by late Thursday night.
talking_points: The game: Dallas led 31-10 late in the third quarter at AT&T Stadium. Per the AP, that's the biggest blown lead in Thanksgiving history.
Per SB Nation, the Cowboys had a better than 97% win probability with under five minutes left, and then Elliott hit from 59 with 2 seconds on the clock.
Brady, calling the game with Kevin Burkhardt, squealed as the kick went through. Fans called it an all-timer and 'generational' meme material, while others joked they didn't need to hear that noise.
It's turning into a pattern: PFN noted it follows Brady's viral reaction to a Deebo Samuel TD just 11 days earlier. The NFL also posted his reaction to QB Joe Milton leading the comeback.
host_questions: Is Brady the broadcaster turning into a better meme machine than Brady the player ever was?
Do we want analysts who lose their minds like fans, or should the booth stay composed?
Where does this squeal rank among the great broadcast reactions of all time?
segments.angle: Debate framing: Brady's booth reactions are either the most authentic thing in sports broadcasting right now or a bit that's starting to wear thin. Two viral moments in 11 days, so which is it?

segments.title: Stuffing the Turkey: The Lions' Most Thanksgiving Celebration Ever
segments.why_trending: After Jahmyr Gibbs' 1-yard touchdown against the Bears, Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown pretended to stuff offensive guard Christian Mahogany like a turkey while he lay on the ground. Underdog NFL's clip of it spread fast.
talking_points: The bit: Mahogany lay on the turf as the 'turkey' while Gibbs and St. Brown did the stuffing, at Ford Field on Thanksgiving Day.
Reactions ranged from 'What did I just watch' to 'gotta be fined for this,' and even a 49ers fan admitted it was genuinely funny.
Detroit has hosted a game on every Thanksgiving since 1945, so it was fitting that the Lions' celebration was about the holiday itself.
The downside: the Lions led 19-10 at halftime but lost to the Bears on the last play.
host_questions: Should this get fined, or is it exactly the kind of fun the league should want on Thanksgiving?
Does a great celebration still count if your team blows the game?
Which lineman gets cast as the turkey next year, and what's the sequel?
segments.angle: An all-time Thanksgiving celebration that came in a loss. Debate whether a celebration should be judged on its own or remembered alongside the final score.

segments.title: Haymitch Eats First: Sunrise on the Reaping Takes the Thanksgiving Box Office
segments.why_trending: The Hunger Games prequel about Haymitch opened to $119.3M domestically last weekend and led Thanksgiving Eve with $15M. Meanwhile, viewers on TikTok are posting their reactions, including confusion over Ampert's death scene.
talking_points: The numbers: a $119.3M domestic opening (the fifth-biggest debut of the year, per Gold Derby), then $12.8M Monday and $16M Tuesday for $148.2M through five days.
Thanksgiving Eve: it led with $15M while new openers Focker-in-Law (about $5M opening day) and Hexed fight for second place.
Deadline credited Lionsgate's marketing with reigniting the franchise.
On TikTok, fans are breaking the movie down, and Ampert's death scene has left at least some viewers puzzled.
host_questions: Is Haymitch the best character the franchise could have built a prequel around?
Why do prequels about a story we already know the ending of keep working?
Is a confusing death scene a flaw, or exactly what gets people talking online?
segments.angle: Is this a story that still had something to say, or a lesson in what a smart marketing campaign can do for a familiar title?

segments.title: A Million Data Centers in the Sky? SpaceX's Starmind Gets the FCC's OK
segments.why_trending: On Nov 25, the FCC gave SpaceX conditional authorization for up to one million Starmind orbital data-center satellites, the first US authorization at that scale. CNN, CNBC, NPR and New Atlas all covered it, and The Neuron led its AI digest with the story.
talking_points: The specs: satellites of 70 to 75 meters, in orbits between 500 and 1,002 km.
The pitch is to get around the power, grid, zoning and permitting limits that hold back data centers on the ground.
The fine print: it's an authorization, not a deployment. SpaceX has to launch a first Starmind satellite by Nov 25, 2033 or the license is forfeited.
Scientists quoted by NPR are skeptical about the economics and about how the chips would shed heat in space.
host_questions: Is putting AI data centers in orbit visionary, or a very expensive way to avoid a zoning board?
If the problem is power and permitting on Earth, is space really the easiest fix?
A million satellites sounds wild, so how would you feel looking up at that night sky?
segments.angle: Hype versus physics: an approval for a million satellites makes a great headline, but with a deadline seven years out and open questions about heat and cost, is this a real plan or a placeholder?
